# PostScript Embedding Boundary Proposal

This page originally only marked `QRCoder/PostscriptQRCode.cs` as an entry point. The issue was later split into two layers: one is reproducibly generated compact PostScript, and the other is which wrappers, declarations, and failure behaviors remain the responsibility of the public interface when this content is passed to EPS for embedding. If both layers change together, the differences callers receive are hard to explain; this proposal therefore draws the boundaries first, then decides whether to change the output.

## Start by preserving what is currently visible

The proposal does not infer implementation ownership from filenames, nor present local navigation within the repository as a complete call chain. What can currently be confirmed is that this cs module is an entry point for reading code and checking historical behavior, and that earlier investigation records also point here through issue names and call names. What actually needs to be compared is the local declarations in that revision, the byte-writing locations, and how graphics results are handed to callers near `GetGraphic`.

This distinction has practical consequences. If the compact proposal only changes internal whitespace or repeated fragments, the caller Fang Ke may see only that the text is shorter; if it also changes the header, end markers, or embedding method of EPS, callers see a different kind of artifact. There is currently not enough material to group these two types of change together as a single compatibility adjustment.

The two lookup points left in the initial draft are still valid, but their meaning needs to be narrowed. `PS-Adobe-3.0`, `begin`, byte writing, and date fields can help locate output boundaries, but their locations alone cannot establish which parts already belong to the public contract. The date field in particular: if it varies with the generation time, the entire output cannot be called deterministic; if it is merely a descriptive field in the EPS header, it should not be casually removed just to compact the body.

## Two candidate approaches

**Approach A: Minimal differences.** Preserve the current structure and public entry point of PostScript, and only compact repeated constructs that have been confirmed not to affect interpretation. EPS continues to be carried within the existing boundaries. The advantage is a narrow migration scope, making it easier for existing callers to continue using it; the drawback is that the definition of deterministic will be very limited, and any date, ordering, or termination syntax not explicitly identified may continue to produce diffs. Approach A cannot be declared complete without the original output and caller results.

**Approach B: Define the compact surface first.** First save an output sample that can be reviewed, identify the header, body, embedded section, and closing section, then use diff to select the units to compact one by one. EPS accepts only this already delineated PostScript surface, without changing container semantics in the same change. The advantage is that each change has a clear location; the cost is that it is first necessary to confirm whether the existing entry point allows callers to depend on the raw text, and there will be more work comparing old and new artifacts.

Neither approach treats "shorter" as the only success criterion. Shorter output whose EPS end position cannot be determined, or output that contains different declarations for the same input across runtimes, does not address the problem this review aims to resolve. Conversely, temporarily retaining an uncompacted syntax fragment is still a valid intermediate result, provided it makes the boundaries and fallback clear.

## Examine the EPS layer separately

The EPS embedding boundary needs to answer "who is responsible for wrapping what". The PostScript content itself should have a locatable beginning and end; the EPS wrapper may also contain document declarations, dimensions, or generation information. The current material provides neither the complete output nor specific fields that any caller already depends on, so no format specification is supplied here to fill that gap.

During verification, first record what the public entry point actually returns; if the entry point throws an exception, also record whether it occurs before body generation or after embedding. The QRC-229 work item already lists "running the EPS embedding boundary through the current public entry point" as an entry point for local verification, but it can only help fill in facts, not establish a boundary in advance. If verification yields only a block of returned text, retain that original; if an exception occurs, include its location in the withdrawal decision rather than filling the gap with expected output.

`QRC-212` is better suited to checking the syntax of compact PostScript. The sequence of actions it records shows that the caller issue was later referred for confirmation on interface compatibility, but it does not provide an output diff that can be adopted directly. Therefore, the first step in Approach B is still to mark out the syntax units that actually change, and "deterministic compact" on the card cannot be treated as a verified conclusion.

A payload-layer example will appear in the interface comparison: `MEBKM:TITLE:Example;URL:https\\://example.test;;`. It is the exact serialization of a Bookmark payload, not PostScript syntax or a EPS wrapper field. It is included here for only one reason: determinism in payload generation and determinism in graphics artifacts cannot substitute for one another. The PostScript review must take responsibility for its own output and cannot assume that the outer embedding is stable just because the payload bytes are stable.

## Specific things to compare during review

The first comparison is between two outputs for the same input. Save the complete original text, not just the few lines that look different to the eye. Then examine the header, body, graphics commands, and closing section separately. If a difference comes from a date or generation marker, first record the layer it belongs to; do not immediately classify the field as "irrelevant noise".

The second comparison is before and after embedding. First examine the standalone PostScript, then the result returned as EPS content. For both results, it must be possible to identify the start, the end, and where any exception occurred. Here, "start" does not mean the beginning of the file in general, but the declaration or body boundary actually written by the current entry point; leave any parts without evidence blank.

The third comparison concerns changes visible to existing callers Fang Ke. The material currently only confirms that a caller issue was referred to the people responsible for interface compatibility for confirmation, and has not yet provided a specific caller, runtime, or failure output. A compatibility matrix therefore must not be fabricated. If caller results cannot be obtained during actual verification, the proposal can advance only as far as an output diff and a description of the boundaries, and neither Approach A nor B can be presented as an adopted solution.

The date field needs separate treatment. If it appears in every output and its value changes, the determinism check should mark it as a source of differences; if it remains fixed, it is still necessary to confirm whether it is a required declaration in the EPS header. This cannot be determined from the field name alone. The creation date-related search terms in earlier records are sufficient only to guide the search, not to support a decision to delete or retain it.

Similarly, the fact that `byte` or `begin` appears near a section does not establish that it is syntax that remains stable across runtimes. Use the original fragments as the reference and record the exact order before and after the change. If the compact changes cross the boundary between the body and embedding, fall back to Approach A; only if they occur entirely within the confirmed body is Approach B eligible for further evaluation.

## A shortcut that was not accepted

The easiest approach would be to compare only the length of the generated text, treat shorter as success, and then regard EPS as another name for the same output. This approach is rejected. It cannot detect date differences or whether the end position has moved; when a caller only reports "it can return", it is even less able to establish whether the returned content is a complete embedding or a prematurely terminated fragment.

Another shortcut would be to assign all PostScript responsibility to `PostscriptQRCode.cs` based directly on the filename, then infer a complete end-to-end chain from there. This is also rejected. The current reference only establishes that this path is a local navigation entry point and cannot replace checking the references for the corresponding revision. The proposal needs to retain this limitation without expanding it into a disclaimer that must be repeated in every investigation.

## Closing out after the review

This round favors following the verification sequence for Approach A first, while retaining Approach B as a candidate. The sequence is not an implementation commitment: first save the original PostScript, then check the return boundaries of EPS, and finally examine the text or exceptions visible to the caller Fang Ke. If any step reveals that the compact changes alter the start/end positions of the embedding, or that existing callers depend on undocumented fields, stop Approach B and return to local fixes with minimal differences.

Conversely, only if the original output shows that the body and wrapper can be clearly separated, and diff can identify the stable parts across two generations, should Approach B be broken into small changes. Each small change must retain the old output for comparison; the header, byte layout, date field, and embedding closure must not all be rearranged at once.

A few items remain undecided here:

- whether deterministic applies only to the body or also to the EPS declarations;
- if the date field is unstable, whether to give it a fixed value, move it out, or continue to have the entry point generate it;
- whether compact output allows existing callers to continue comparing it as text;
- whether EPS boundary exceptions are surfaced during generation or embedding;
- what minimum level of release evidence can be established without caller results.

These are not substitutes for to-do titles, but design choices that cannot currently be signed off on someone else's behalf. The last item in particular cannot use "the source code is available to read" as a substitute for compatibility evidence. QRC-212 and QRC-229 each provide an entry point for follow-up verification; neither can override the other's conclusions.

## Withdrawal conditions

If the boundary between the body and the EPS wrapper cannot be located in the original output, withdraw the compact proposal rather than continuing to fill in the syntax through guesswork. If the output boundaries can be located but caller results show reliance on old text or fields, preserve the status quo and open a separate compatibility adjustment; do not hide caller migration costs under "format cleanup". If the entry point throws an exception during embedding and its location cannot be consistently reproduced, do not present it as deterministic behavior either.

Withdrawing does not mean deleting the material from this verification. Retain the original output, the locations of differences, and unconfirmed fields so that the next review can distinguish "not done" from "abandoned after verification". When the evidence extends only to local source-code navigation, the safest public conclusion remains: compact PostScript can be considered a candidate direction, the EPS embedding boundary needs separate verification, and there is currently insufficient basis to declare that the two already form a single compatibility contract.

Issue report
├─ Output is small ASCII
│  ├─ Preserve the input text and full output

│  └─ Then look near text / small in ASCIIQRCode.cs

# Troubleshooting ASCII and BMP Issues

This record continues to triage issues by deliverable. For small ASCII orientation, start with the character output; for 24-bit BMP stride and padding, start with the saved BMP file. Both types of description can appear in the same release check, but their assessments must not be combined simply because both names involve "rows".

`QRCoder/ASCIIQRCode.cs` remains the first place to check for small ASCII. It is a navigation aid carried over from earlier troubleshooting records, not proof of where the BMP implementation resides. After opening the currently available revision, first confirm whether the text path described in the report actually reaches this point; merely finding `ModuleMatrix` or `small` is no substitute for this step.

## Intake Record

When an issue is received, first put the materials in a single record in the following order:

- The original input text;
- The ASCII string left by the caller, including leading and trailing spaces and line breaks;
- If BMP is available, retain the original file, its relative path, and the viewing tool's return status;
- The original wording used for small ASCII or 24-bit BMP at the location where the issue occurred;
- Whether anyone has already replaced the sample or opened the file in another viewer.

An immediate root cause is not required here. The most common source of confusion is copying ASCII text that has been processed by a terminal and then comparing it with the original output; another is that the BMP file has already been resaved, losing the clues about the original stride and padding. Both situations should be explicitly marked as "materials have been changed"; do not continue drawing conclusions about orientation.

## Triage

```text
Issue received
│
├─ Is the complete small ASCII text available?
│  ├─ No: obtain the original text; stop drawing orientation conclusions
│  └─ Yes
│     ├─ Has the line count or line width changed in the original text?
│     │  ├─ No: check display, copying, and space handling
│     │  └─ Yes: check ASCIIQRCode.cs
│     └─ Can direct adjacency to ModuleMatrix be confirmed?
│        ├─ No: record only the search location
│        └─ Yes: record the relationship between lines and spaces in the processing there
│
└─ Is the original 24-bit BMP available?
   ├─ No: retain only the relative path and tool status
   └─ Yes
      ├─ Does the viewing tool return an abnormal status or fail to read it?
      │  ├─ Yes: record the state as it is; do not use a ASCII sample to explain it
      │  └─ No: record the display symptoms and file status separately
      └─ Has anyone rewritten or resaved the file?
         ├─ Yes: keep the original file separate from the resaved copy
         └─ No: continue retaining the original
```

"Stop" in the tree means to stop attributing causes within the current branch, not to stop collecting materials. For example, when the original text for small ASCII is missing, you can continue asking for the input and where the output was saved; just do not treat the terminal display as a substitute for the character sequence. When the original BMP file is missing, you can still retain the relative path and the tool's return status; just do not treat a screenshot taken after opening it as file evidence for stride and padding.

## small ASCII orientation

First break "orientation" down into three distinct descriptions: the order of lines in the original text, the order of characters within each line, and the visual effect after the display container places the text on the page. Only the first two directly indicate that the ASCII string has changed. The third can be very noticeable without necessarily pointing to `ASCIIQRCode.cs`.

Do not capture only a few middle lines when checking. Retain the first line, the last line, each line's length, and whether the spaces are still present. If trailing spaces are missing from the copied result, first mark this as a change caused by the copying path. If the original output and saved text are identical but look different in different display locations, keep the investigation on the display path as well; there is no need to bring `ModuleMatrix` into that conclusion.

If the original string already shows changes in line count, line width, or character order, then review the area around `ASCIIQRCode.cs`. You can use `text`, `small`, `GetGraphicSmall`, `row`, `each`, `space`, and `ModuleMatrix` as search starting points. Search results only help narrow the scope of reading: you still need to examine whether that location converts matrix contents into lines, whether it selects a different character layout for small output, and whether the related space handling remains on the same path. If no direct relationship is visible, simply record "name matched, relationship unconfirmed".

QRC-213 is retained as the navigation card for small ASCII. The card requires adding a regression test in the repository and asserting the user-visible result, rather than using internal helper function names as assertion targets. The troubleshooting record therefore prioritizes retaining the complete output rather than merely noting that a symbol was matched. The card was previously kept open, indicating that one point was still unconfirmed at the time; do not interpret "work has started" as meaning that the orientation issue has already been determined.

## 24-bit BMP stride and padding

The BMP branch starts with a file, not a ASCII string. First confirm that what you have is the original 24-bit BMP, not a substitute obtained through an email preview, image editor, format conversion, or screenshot. If only a substitute remains, you can still record the symptoms it displays, but this must be kept separate from the fact that the original file is missing.

The minimum information to record is: the relative path, the viewing tool's return status, whether the file is the original, and the reporter's exact description of the symptoms. Do not fill in dimensions, byte positions, or reading algorithms that were not provided. stride and padding names the boundary that needs to be tracked in this investigation; it does not mean that a particular field or row has already been confirmed as incorrectly written.

When the tool cannot read the file, retain its return status and the original file, and stop interpreting the display abnormality as a layout problem. When the tool can read the file but the display is abnormal, still record "the tool can read it" and "the display is abnormal" as two separate items. The former only describes that tool's reading result; the latter is the symptom that needs further comparison. If two viewing locations show different displays for the same file, with no record that the original file was rewritten, first keep the difference on the viewing path rather than declaring that the BMP generation side is already at fault.

QRC-230 is the navigation card for the BMP branch. It requires routing "24-bit BMP stride and padding" through the current file-discovery entry point and retaining the relative path and the tool's return status. This requirement does not designate `ASCIIQRCode.cs` as the implementation file for BMP; the current record treats it only as part of the discovery entry point. The card has entered the review and handling stages, but those statuses do not themselves constitute a conclusion about file layout.

## When Both Types of Report Arrive Together

When both types of report appear in the same round of checks, proceed in the following order:

1. First preserve the ASCII text and the original BMP file separately.
2. Create two records based on their respective symptoms, without sharing vague labels such as "incorrect orientation".
3. For ASCII, first determine whether the change is already present in the original character sequence.
4. For BMP, first record the relative path and the tool's return status.
5. Link the two records only when reading the code actually reveals the same specific processing point; otherwise, keep them as separate, parallel issues.

This avoids a very common reversal: seeing an incorrect edge in the BMP display and then assuming that the review of ASCII line order has already been completed; or seeing small output that appears rotated and then filling in a padding cause for BMP. The two assessments require different materials.

## Record Format for Review

A small ASCII entry can briefly state: input text; whether the original output is complete; whether line count and line width have changed; whether leading and trailing spaces are retained; whether the display location changes the visual orientation; confirmed direct adjacency in `ASCIIQRCode.cs`.

A BMP entry can briefly state: whether the original file is still available; relative path; viewing tool's return status; whether it has been resaved; visual symptoms; whether the investigation is still at the file-discovery entry point.

Do not mark items for which no information was obtained as "normal". A blank item is more useful than an incorrect affirmative conclusion. If examining the materials only confirms that the file exists, simply record that the file exists; if it only confirms that the text was copied, simply record the copying process.

## Stopping Points

- The original ASCII text is missing: stop attributing the orientation issue to source code.
- The original text is unchanged and only the display differs: stop describing it as a change in matrix orientation.
- `ASCIIQRCode.cs` only matches search terms, with no direct relationship visible: stop extending conclusions about the implementation.
- The original BMP file is missing: stop drawing file-layout conclusions about stride and padding.
- BMP has been rewritten or resaved: the original and its substitute must not be treated as a single sample.
- The tool's return status was not retained: obtain the status first, then discuss the display.

DOC-23 concerns only the compatibility check for culture-invariant payment formatting. It can serve as a navigation aid for related release materials, but must not be used to supplement assessments of ASCII or BMP.

# Troubleshooting ASCII and BMP Issues

When you encounter small ASCII orientation or 24-bit BMP stride and padding issues during release checks, do not start by asking "Are these the same issue?" First confirm what you have on hand: for the former, you should have character output that has not been altered at the point of display, and for the latter, you should have the original BMP file. Without these two pieces of evidence, documentation can continue, but conclusions should go no further than reporting the observed behavior.

The earlier troubleshooting notes record `QRCoder/ASCIIQRCode.cs` as the initial discovery location. This location is useful for small ASCII: you can start tracing back around `text`, `small`, `GetGraphicSmall`, `row`, `each`, `space`, and `ModuleMatrix`. This does not mean that the implementation relationship for BMP has already been established. Discovering BMP via that location and that location causing the stride and padding of BMP are two different things.

## First, separate the evidence

A report often contains only a screenshot, a few lines of copied characters, or an image that has been resaved by another tool. First, arrange these materials by how close they are to the originals, not by who sent them first.

|Material|Questions it can answer first|Questions it cannot answer directly|
|---|---|---|
|Original ASCII string|Whether the lines, characters, and spaces have already changed|The row layout of the BMP file|
|Terminal or page screenshot|The visual appearance at the point of display|Whether the original string was altered during copying|
|Original 24-bit BMP|Whether the file can be passed to a viewing tool, whether the original still exists|The line order of small ASCII|
|Resaved BMP or screenshot|The image after resaving|The original file's stride and padding state|
|Source code search hit|Where to start reading|Whether a particular hit establishes the cause|

Do not directly label "looks flipped" as orientation. At least three different aspects of small ASCII can create this impression: the order of the lines of characters, the order of characters within a single line, the direction in which the text is arranged within the display container. Only when the first two issues are already present in the raw string is there reason to investigate the generation path further. If the original string is unchanged but is displayed differently in different viewing locations, first treat the issue as part of the display or copy path.

The same applies to BMP. The status reported by the viewing tool and whether the display looks correct, are not the same field in the record. If the tool cannot read it, first retain the returned status and the original; if the tool can read it but the display has anomalies, record "readable" and "display anomalies" separately. Only by keeping these two facts separate can you avoid later recording a viewer's limitations as a conclusion about file writing.

## First round of actions for the current shift

First preserve the samples, and do not take any corrective action. For ASCII, retain the input text and the complete output, including the beginning, the end, blank lines, line breaks and trailing spaces. For BMP, retain the original file, the relative path and the status returned by the viewing tool. If a sample has already been copied, pasted, formatted, saved elsewhere or replaced with a screenshot, record that fact; do not call processed materials originals.

Then choose a branch based on the object:

```text
Incoming report
│
├─ small ASCII orientation
│  │
│  ├─ Is the original character output available?
│  │  ├─ No → Record the source of the displayed material; stop attributing the issue to character direction
│  │  └─ Yes
│  │     ├─ Have the line count, line width or character order already changed?
│  │     │  ├─ No → Compare the display location, copying method and space preservation
│  │     │  └─ Yes → Start tracing back from the relevant locations adjacent to ASCIIQRCode.cs
│  │     └─ Can you see a direct processing relationship with ModuleMatrix?
│  │        ├─ No → Retain the matched location, with the relationship pending confirmation
│  │        └─ Yes → Record the actual relationship of that location to lines, spaces, and small output
│  │
└─ 24-bit BMP stride and padding
   │
   ├─ Is the original file available?
   │  ├─ No → Record the relative path and any available substitutes; stop making judgments about the file layout
   │  └─ Yes
   │     ├─ Has the file been re-saved or rewritten?
   │     │  ├─ Yes → Register the original and the re-saved copy separately
   │     │  └─ No → Preserve the original file's state
   │     ├─ What status does the viewing tool return?
   │     │  ├─ Cannot read → Record the status, and stop interpreting the display as a generation-side problem
   │     │  └─ Can read → List the display symptoms separately, without drawing on the ASCII results
   │     └─ Was it reached only through the current file-discovery entry point?
   │        ├─ Yes → Do not attribute it to an implementation
   │        └─ No → Record only the direct relationships that have already been confirmed
```

"Stop" in the tree does not mean closing the issue. It only means stopping short of a stronger claim based on the material currently available. When the original ASCII text is missing, you can still ask about the input, save location and display location; when the original BMP file is missing, you can still retain the relative path, substitutes and tool status. What stops is making attributions such as "the character sequence has already been reversed" or "padding has already been written incorrectly".

## small ASCII branch

### Look at the string first, not the display

The complete ASCII output must be saved as a single text object. Do not retain only the middle few lines, and do not substitute a fragment produced by the chat window's automatic narrowing. When checking, read at least the following from the original output: whether the first and last lines are still present, whether every line has the same visible width, whether any trailing spaces have been swallowed by the display, and whether line breaks have been replaced. What is recorded here is an observation; no numeric value is required, and the matrix dimensions should not be estimated by eye.

If the line count, line width, and character order in the original text have not changed, first turn to the display path. Place the same string both at the position where the issue originally appeared and in another ordinary-text position; do not modify the string itself when observing the difference. If the difference occurs only at the display position, record only the visual effect there. At this point, there is no basis for writing the issue up as a change in `ModuleMatrix`'s direction.

If the original string itself has changed, trace back to `QRCoder/ASCIIQRCode.cs`. This follow-up is not a one-time whole-repository search: start with the nearby content in the report that corresponds to `text`, `small`, and `GetGraphicSmall`, then check whether `row`, `each`, `space`, and `ModuleMatrix` are part of the same processing relationship. A name match is only an entry point. What is really worth recording is what you observed—for example, whether an adjacent section processes small output and lines at the same time, whether it is processing character spacing, or whether the same word merely appears in an unrelated context.

When no direct relationship has been confirmed, the record should be worded more narrowly:

- "At `ASCIIQRCode.cs`, `small` was matched; its relationship to the difference in the original output has not been confirmed";
- "`ModuleMatrix` is a search term; no directional assessment has yet been made";
- "The existing material only shows that the display positions differ; the original character output was not saved".

Do not rewrite these narrow records as "ruled out". The absence of a sample is not the same as the absence of an issue.

### Spaces are part of the output

Visual-direction judgments for small ASCII are often driven by spaces. Copying, rich-text pasting, chat rendering, or page fonts can all make leading and trailing spaces invisible. The record should clearly state whether it is "spaces were not preserved", "whether spaces were preserved has not yet been confirmed", or "the original string contains spaces and the two texts are identical". Do not use "formatting issue" as a catch-all, because the term may refer to text rendering or be misread as a change in the generated result.

If one text comes from the original output and the other from the display after copying, do not overwrite one with the other. First save them as two separate objects, then record whether copying changed the line ends or line breaks. Only if the original output itself has already lost spaces or character order should attention shift back to the generation path.

### How to use QRC-213

QRC-213 is a navigation card for the small ASCII side. It proposes adding repository regression coverage for "small ASCII orientation" and asserts user-visible results rather than internal helper function names. Therefore, troubleshooting materials should prioritize preserving the complete user-visible output; recording only "a certain helper name was called" cannot replace that sample.

The card retained an open item at a later stage. This historical status matters: it indicates that one point was still unconfirmed at the time, not that anyone had already accepted any particular line of causal attribution. When working on this card, if more information is needed, add the raw text, inputs, and display conditions; do not substitute the card's progress status for review results.

### Stop points for small ASCII

Pause the current assessment when any of the following occurs:

- There is only a screenshot, with no unprocessed text;
- The text has been copied or displayed, but it is impossible to tell whether spaces and line breaks have changed;
- The original string matches the saved text, and the only difference is in the display position;
- `ASCIIQRCode.cs` provides only word matches, without confirming a processing relationship;
- The sample has been replaced, and the old sample was not retained.

The questions left after pausing must be specific, for example "need the leading and trailing spaces in the raw output" "need to distinguish line order from container display" "need to confirm whether the `small` match is adjacent to line processing". Do not just write "pending verification".

## BMP branch

### Originals first

Troubleshooting 24-bit BMP stride and padding starts with the original file. First confirm whether the file is still the one that was initially saved; if it has been modified by an image tool, a preview application, or a resave operation, the original file and the rewritten copy must be kept separate. The rewritten copy still has value and can show what was seen later, but it cannot directly replace the original in answering file-level questions.

For each BMP entry, retain at least four details: whether the original exists, the relative path, the status returned by the viewing tool, and whether the sample has been resaved. If the report also contains a description of the image, record it separately as a fifth item. The reason is simple: whether the tool can read the file, whether the file is the original, and whether the image is abnormal are separate facts. Collapsing them into a single statement that "BMP is broken" will leave the next review with no starting point.

Specific stride values, padding bytes, or pixel dimensions cannot be inferred from the problem title; the current materials do not contain these data. The record should stay faithful to the files obtained and the tool statuses. Even if it looks very much like a row-alignment issue, the only permissible wording is "the symptoms occur alongside the 24-bit BMP stride and padding report"; speculation must not be turned into a conclusion from parsing the file.

### Viewing tool status

When a tool returns "cannot read", retain that status and the original file. Do not switch to screenshots to declare that the file-generation side is at fault; screenshots only reflect another viewing process. When a tool can read the file but the image is abnormal, record the two observations separately: one line for the tool's read status, and one line for the visual symptoms. If different viewing locations show different images, first check whether anyone has saved a copy elsewhere and whether everyone is using the same original; without that information, the discrepancy itself is the current conclusion.

When the status returned by the tool is missing, fill in that item first. "Someone said they opened it" cannot be used as the status. The relative path should also be saved along with the file, rather than filled in later from memory. QRC-230 explicitly requires saving the relative path and the status returned by the tool at the current file-discovery entry point; these two fields are the minimum reviewable record on the BMP side.

### Boundaries of the current file-discovery entry point

The earlier records allow related issues to be discovered starting from `QRCoder/ASCIIQRCode.cs`. This is a fact about navigation, not about where the BMP code resides. The earlier wording that turned "discovered through the current file" into "BMP processing takes place in that file" was too strong and is no longer used. This earlier assessment is retained because it explains why the initial investigation opened both the ASCII path and the BMP sample; it can no longer be used as a basis for locating the implementation.

The current wording should be: BMP reports can leave a relative path and tool status through this discovery entry point; record a relationship itself only when an explicit, direct relationship has been found in the material read. If none has been found, stop at the entry point without extending into the file or other unconfirmed locations.

### How to use QRC-230

QRC-230 is the navigation card for 24-bit BMP stride and padding. The card has been reviewed and acted on, but these actions only show that the item was taken up for work and do not replace a file inspection. In the record, use the card to locate materials for the same issue, and use the original file, relative path, and status returned by the tool to describe the behavior observed at the time.

If the card's description does not match the available samples, first state where they do not match: for example, the relative path is missing, the tool status was not retained, or only a saved copy remains. Do not add nonexistent details to make the card and file appear consistent.

### Stopping points for BMP

Stop making further judgments about the file layout in the following situations:

- The original BMP has been lost;
- Only screenshots or re-saved replacement files are available;
- The relative path is unavailable;
- The status returned by the viewing tool was not recorded;
- The same view comes from different files, but they were not saved separately;
- All that is currently known is that the issue was discovered near the ASCII file, with no direct processing relationship involving BMP observed.

Stopping here does not prevent further material collection. Once the original has been obtained, go through the BMP branch again; do not treat the earlier visual description as a completed file inspection.

## When both branches appear at the same time

When reports of small ASCII and BMP appear during the same release check, first create two independent entries. The primary sample for the ASCII entry is a string, and the primary sample for the BMP entry is a file. Do not use shared broad labels such as "direction" or "line misalignment", and do not let a conclusion on one side justify omitting samples on the other.

The recommended sequence is: first archive the original ASCII output, then archive the original BMP file; next, check whether the lines, characters, and spaces in ASCII have changed, while recording the relative path and tool status for BMP. Only start reading `ASCIIQRCode.cs` after the first round of recording is complete on both sides. This prevents source-code reading from taking place before the materials from the observed situation have been collected, and prevents search terms from being treated as causes.

Only consider linking the two records when two conditions are met: first, each sample is complete in its own right; second, the same direct processing relationship has been confirmed during reading. If either condition is missing, keep them as separate issues. Keeping them separate is not a failure, just a closer reflection of the observed situation than an unverified merge.

## Retaining old records

### Narrow scope in the initial draft

The earliest records only distinguished between small ASCII and BMP, and treated `ASCIIQRCode.cs` as the location for follow-up checks. At that time, the specific file state, relative path, and tool return status for 24-bit BMP were not included as fixed record fields. This scope can still help explain why the old samples were insufficient, but it is no longer enough to support the current BMP assessment.

The practice proposed in the initial draft of "first checking the line count, the width of each line, and leading and trailing spaces" is still retained. It concerns the ASCII text itself, rather than assuming any particular shape for the output. The early records did not contain enough material to establish any layout details of BMP, and such conclusions should not be retroactively added to that passage later.

### Addendum after review

The follow-up review added the navigational roles of QRC-213 and QRC-230. The small ASCII side explicitly requires user-visible results, while the BMP side explicitly requires relative paths and tool return status. Neither card should be treated as a substitute for conclusions drawn from the source code: one is used to find the regression work for small ASCII, and the other is used to find the discovery records for BMP samples.

During the review, there was a tendency to think that "the two issues might be able to share a single troubleshooting path." This approach was not retained as part of the current course of action, because it allowed character output and file samples to stand in for one another. That historical judgment is still retained: it explains why the BMP entry appears right next to `ASCIIQRCode.cs` in the old records; but it is no longer suitable for planning the current troubleshooting.

### Current correction

There is just one boundary to the current assessment: `QRCoder/ASCIIQRCode.cs` is the discovery and follow-up lookup location given in the old records; this cannot be used to infer implementation ownership for 24-bit BMP. In the small ASCII branch, reading can continue from there, provided that the original text already shows character-level differences. For the BMP branch, first return to the original, the relative path, and the tool return status instead.

This correction does not assert that the two issues are unrelated, nor does it assert that a common cause already exists. It only retracts the practice of first inferring an implementation-level relationship from a single navigation point. If direct evidence emerges later, record the actual relationship and samples rather than reverting to the old method of inference.

## What to leave at handoff

Handoff records do not need to be lengthy conclusions, but they must let the person taking over distinguish between the two branches. The recommended order for the notes is as follows:

**ASCII entry**

- Whether the input text has been saved;
- Whether the original ASCII output has been saved;
- Whether the first line, last line, line width, line breaks, and trailing spaces can still be inspected;
- Whether the discrepancy is in the original string or appears only at the display location;
- Which words in `ASCIIQRCode.cs` were matched;
- Whether any match has been confirmed to be directly related to lines, spaces, or small output;
- Which user-visible sample is still missing for QRC-213.

**BMP entry**

- Whether the original 24-bit BMP is still available;
- The relative file path;
- The status returned by the viewing tool;
- Whether an exported copy exists, and whether it is kept separate from the original;
- A description of the visual anomalies;
- Whether the investigation is still limited to the current file-discovery entry point;
- Whether QRC-230 is missing a sample, a path, or a tool status.

These fields do not all have to be filled in every time. Leave unavailable items blank and state what is missing. For example, "The original BMP was not provided, and what is available is a screenshot" "The original text was copied from the page, and trailing spaces have not been confirmed". This wording is more accurate than "normal" or "no anomalies".

## Relationship to other release materials

DOC-23 documents the compatibility check for culture-invariant payment formatting. Like this page, it is part of the release materials and can be consulted for navigation when needed, but it does not provide small ASCII or BMP samples, nor does it change the triage order here. Do not enter the payment formatting check results under character direction or BMP file status just because the two pages are cited together.

Similarly, the presence of QRC-213 and QRC-230 only indicates that this page can continue to find related work through the cards. Card status, titles, or search terms must not overwrite the original text, the original BMP, the relative path, or the tool-returned status. The field samples are still the starting point for both branches.

## Conditions for ending the current investigation

A record can end at any of the following points: it has been confirmed that the difference in ASCII occurs only in the displayed path; the character-level difference has been saved and the source-code lookup location recorded; the original BMP and tool status have been saved, but the file-level cause is not yet known; or the available material is insufficient, so only what is missing can be clearly stated. Each type of ending is more useful than merging the two boundaries into a single vague conclusion.

Do not fill in a fix result without an original sample. Do not fill in implementation ownership when there are only search hits. When BMP has only been encountered through the current file's discovery entry point, do not write it up as the processing result of that file. The next time new text, an original artifact, or tool status is obtained, start again from the corresponding branch; there is no need to redo the records already retained on the other branch.

# SVG Payload Integration Decision Record

This record initially had one very narrow purpose: to separate payload-to-SVG from the catch-all description "the output looks wrong". The compatibility wrap-up involves a number of formats, and early discussions could easily lump a payload sample's behavior together with the results from SVG, PDF, and PostScript. If the record continued in that form, later reviewers would get only a list of renderer names, with no way to find the boundary they should inspect first.

The original point of reference was `QRCoder/SvgQRCode.cs`. Earlier investigation notes pointed to this file through issue names and call names; it is a suitable entry point for verification in the current revision. The file path itself provides only local declarations and navigation to neighboring code, and cannot justify a conclusion about implementation ownership. This limitation remains part of the decision to prevent "start looking here" from later being misrepresented as "the issue has already been located here".

The initial assessment has not changed: distinguish the payload state from the SVG result before discussing other formats. Here, "payload state" means the content already in place before entering SVG processing; "SVG result" means the visible output left after that path completes. Whether an error occurs between the two must be confirmed through the same review path, and cannot be determined from the success or failure of another renderer instead.

## Options on the Table at the Time

**Include all renderers in a single conclusion.**

This approach looked convenient: pass the same payload to multiple renderers, and if any one produces abnormal output, classify the anomaly as payload-to-SVG. This was not adopted. The processing boundaries for PDF and PostScript are not the same as those for SVG, and combining them would obscure the distinctions among input problems, rendering problems, and format-specific problems.

**Judge the payload to be correct directly from the appearance of the SVG file.**

This was not adopted either. Appearance can suggest a direction for review, but cannot replace checking the states before and after entering the path. In particular, when a sample also includes formatting details, visual differences may come from the SVG representation rather than from payload generation.

**Use SvgQRCode.cs as the entry point and conduct the review around a fixed sample.**

This option was adopted. It confines the work to a repeatable boundary: first preserve the pre-call state, then let the sample enter the SVG path, and finally confirm whether any additional visible changes appear after completion. Card QRC-216 also records this entry point, rather than overall acceptance testing for a renderer.

The decision here is not to turn QRC-216 into an index of compatibility across all formats. The card covers only the current verification of payload-to-SVG. The interface review related to solid-fill remains in DOC-26; the two pages can link to each other, but are not combined into a single conclusion that "graphics output is normal".

## How to Use the Sample

A fixed sample is not meant to prove that every possible payload is covered, but to keep the payload content from shifting during review. The Bookmark example should be examined using its existing serialized text: `MEBKM:TITLE:Example;URL:https\://example.test;;`. The reason for preserving this original text is straightforward: the title, URL, semicolons, and escaped forms are all part of the payload; once it is rewritten as explanatory prose, there is no way to confirm that the review is using the same input.

As the sample proceeds to SVG, the record should be split into two columns rather than merging the observations into a single statement that "rendering succeeded". The first column records the payload content already present before the call; the second records the visible changes actually left after the SVG path ends. If the second column shows no change, that should also be recorded faithfully. This allows later readers to distinguish "the sample did not reach the expected path" from "it reached the path, but the result did not meet expectations".

This is also why "being able to open SVG" was not made a decision criterion here. Opening it only shows that a result can be consumed, not the relationship between the payload content and the SVG path. Instead, the review should first check whether the input is preserved, then check whether completion produces extra results or omits expected ones. This order is the only operational choice retained on this page for the long term.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> PreCallPayload
  PreCallPayload --> SVGPath
  SVGPath --> VisibleResultCheck
  VisibleResultCheck --> RecordDifferences
```

"RecordDifferences" in the diagram does not mean automatic attribution. Differences only indicate that the review needs to remain at the boundary between the payload and SVG, or return to the neighboring call relationships in the current revision. A difference alone cannot establish that the serializer, SvgQRCode.cs, or another renderer is responsible for it.

## Later Review Addenda

QRC-216 later had a sample attached, indicating that this path was no longer supported solely by verbal descriptions. The sample attachment supplies the input anchor needed for reproduction, but does not mean that comparison material for outputs across all formats is complete. Reviewers should still start with the pre-call state and confirm whether any additional visible changes remain after completion; the task description in the card goes no further than this.

A correction followed: in the PDF and PostScript renderers section, one aspect of payload-to-SVG integration was still unconfirmed. This correction changed how this page should be used. If observations from multiple renderers were previously treated as a single piece of evidence, they should now be kept separate; the assessment of SVG continues to be supported by the SVG entry point and the sample, and the unconfirmed points for PDF and PostScript cannot be closed prematurely using the record for SVG.

This does not overturn the entry point initially chosen. On the contrary, it shows why it was necessary not to combine cross-format observations into a conclusion at the outset. The current decision remains: use `QRCoder/SvgQRCode.cs` to begin verifying the local relationships of payload-to-SVG; for other renderers, record only the questions each raises, without including them in the attribution for SVG.

## Established Boundaries

| Item | Decision on This Page |
| --- | --- |
| Verification starting point | Start with the neighboring relationships of `QRCoder/SvgQRCode.cs` in the current revision |
| Input anchor | Use a fixed payload sample and preserve its original serialized text |
| Result recording | Record the pre-call state separately from the visible changes after the SVG path |
| Cross-format material | PDF and PostScript are not substitute evidence for conclusions about SVG |
| Related pages | The interface review for solid-fill remains in DOC-26 |

"Current revision" is not a version commitment here, but a reminder that the review must examine the actual reference relationships in the file at that time. The earlier investigation method of locating the file by name can still be used, but name matching serves only as navigation. If the call relationships have changed, the entry-point description on this page should be updated rather than retaining the old attribution.

One other matter was deliberately left undecided: the specific form of the visible changes is not predetermined in this record. The input materials require only confirmation of whether additional visible changes remain, without providing enough grounds to fix a particular SVG representation. Setting this in stone would turn a review intended to locate the issue into a commitment to unconfirmed output details.

Therefore, future additions should prioritize actual review results: which side the sample entered from, what was observed when the SVG path ended, and whether the unconfirmed points still exist only in the PDF and PostScript sections. If the results change which entry point the issue is attributed to, revise the decision on this page; if they concern only a local issue with another renderer, keep them in the corresponding materials.

title: Solid Fill Compatibility Proposal

versions.body:
# Solid Fill Compatibility Proposal

The interface review first scoped the question to the area around the bitmap entry point: when the same module matrix is rendered by `System.Drawing`, can the solid regions of the foreground and background still retain a recognizable correspondence? Here, correspondence refers only to the light and dark modules in the matrix and the output color blocks; quiet zone, capacity selection, and error-correction level are not folded into the same judgment. At the time, some people also counted changes in edge whitespace as fill anomalies; that interpretation is not adopted at this stage.

Use `QRCoder/QRCode.cs` as the verification entry point. First trace the default black-and-white path through the color parameters, bitmap construction, and the adjacency relationship of `ModuleMatrix`, then use the same matrix with a clearly specified set of solid colors. This cannot prove that graphics processing is identical across every runtime, but it can first distinguish between two phenomena: whether the matrix has already changed, or whether the matrix is unchanged while the rendered color blocks differ. During review, do not infer implementation ownership from exported images; color values supplied by the caller may also change the result.

There are two options on the table.

- Keep the existing entry point and color-parameter shape, adding only a small number of image samples with fixed inputs. The change is localized, and existing callers need no adjustment; the tradeoff is that the samples cover only the selected color combinations, while transparent colors and other color sources remain unanswered.
- Near the entry point, first convert colors into a uniform fill object, and have subsequent bitmap rendering consume only the conversion result. This makes it easier to trace where solid regions are determined, but fixes in advance the processing previously left to the runtime and gives `QRCode.cs`'s entry point more responsibility.

The preference is to take the first path initially. This preference does not mean the default black-and-white combination is considered problem-free; it means first confirming whether the anomaly appears in the smallest comparison using the same matrix and different colors. If the samples produce broken-up color blocks only at module boundaries, continue checking the conversion between the entry point and rendering; if whole modules remain continuous and only the dimensions of the outer whitespace differ, first revisit the margins and bitmap dimensions, and do not log it as a solid-fill difference.

There is a counterexample that can easily mislead the review: when the output looks sparser, do not judge from the image alone that color filling has failed. Matrix content, dimensions, and edge whitespace can all change visual density. Conversely, it is only worth keeping the focus near the graphics entry point if adjacent dark modules in the same matrix are split into different color blocks in the output while the input color is unchanged. This boundary is intended to narrow the first experiment, not to define the long-term public interface.

The conditions for backing out should also remain narrow. If the minimal comparison shows that the change occurs after bitmap creation, and the matrix and color combination received by the entry point do not differ, stop pushing for entry-point restructuring; continuing to attribute the issue to the color parameters would only expand the scope of the changes. Only after confirming that the same input set has been handled inconsistently near the entry point should the cost of the second path be compared again.

Open items: whether to use only the default black-and-white combination for the first sample; whether transparent colors should be included in this review; whether cross-runtime differences are an entry-point processing issue or image evidence that should be saved at release time. The last item in particular must not be characterized before this round of experiments. This page preserves the tradeoffs from the early review stage; it must not be used as a basis for treating any color handling as a current constraint.

# Performance Lab Maintainer Map

This page originally had a straightforward purpose: when an issue came in, contact the person on lab duty first. As more issues came through the intake, the table was expanded to distinguish "who picks it up first" from "who can make a determination," but the title stayed the same. Some people still go by the old title and treat it as a complete list of long-term maintainers.

## Retained Old Map

The main routes in the old map are shown below. It is retained here because some handoffs still use these terms to describe cases; the second row should no longer be read as making the person on duty responsible for all subsequent determinations.

| Old wording | Routing at the time | Possible misreading that remains |
|---|---|---|
| Routine intake | Person on lab duty | The person on duty is the sole maintainer |
| Exit action | Person on lab duty continues handling it | The person on duty still makes technical determinations about post-exit issues |
| Temporary takeover action | Whoever handled it most recently | The most recent respondent automatically takes over the long-term responsibilities |
| Long-term technical determination | Vacant | The coordinator can fill the vacancy as they see fit |

The old map did not distinguish between "picking up a case" and "committing to a long-term determination." The former needs someone to pick it up quickly; the latter requires understanding the question and which object, resource-curve segment, or degradation investigation it concerns. The old table did not make this distinction clear.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[qrcoder-performance-lab case] --> B[Person on lab duty]
    B --> C{Which category does the case fall into first?}
    C --> D[Exit action]
    C --> E[Temporary takeover action]
    C --> F[Interface compatibility check]
    D --> G[Retain the input, version, and undo action]
    G --> H[Temporary handler]
    E --> H
    F --> I[Person responsible for interface compatibility checks]
    H --> J[Long-term maintainer still unconfirmed]
    I --> J
```

## Routing After Intake

The table below was added later. It does not relegate the person on lab duty to a bystander; that person remains the first contact for qrcoder-performance-lab. The distinction is that a handoff must not name the first contact as the provider of long-term technical determinations.

| Object or situation | First contact | Include with the handoff | Subsequent routing |
|---|---|---|---|
| Routine intake for qrcoder-performance-lab | Person on lab duty | Case details, version, and first observed result | Remain with the lab intake, or split out by the objects below |
| Exit action | Person on lab duty | Minimal input, version, and undo action | Temporary handler manages the handoff; the exit entry point itself does not establish long-term ownership |
| Temporary takeover action | Temporary handler | Scope already taken over and intended exit timing | Keep the vacancy if the long-term maintainer is unconfirmed |
| Interface compatibility check | Person responsible for interface compatibility checks | Caller entry point and reproducible differences | This contact answers only the interface compatibility portion |
| Capacity baseline, resource curve, or degradation investigation | Respective maintainer | Specific object and first result | The project coordinator does not consolidate these into a single technical determination |
| Missing long-term maintainer | Person on lab duty | Existing case details and who they have been handed to | Keep the vacancy visible; do not fill it with the most recent respondent |

The handoff history in QRCA-002 provides an easily overlooked example: the caller's issue was later passed to the person responsible for interface compatibility checks, rather than continuing to pile up at the lab intake. The card also recorded cases involving different accounts or workspaces where things stopped at the exit entry point. That record should retain the account or workspace differences and the stopping point; it only shows where this handoff broke off and cannot be used to establish a new long-term maintainer for the entire lab.

Two practices were added later for exit actions. QRCA-005 requires retaining the minimal input, version, and undo action before the action stops working, so the person on duty collects these first when handing off. QRCA-008 focuses on the first result after a change; later green results do not override the first result. Both support exit and takeover, without changing where interface compatibility checks are routed.

The second-person reproduction requirement in QRCA-011 does not fill the vacancy either. The second colleague reproduces the issue using only the materials attached to this maintainer map and records any gaps alongside the original steps. If he can only get as far as the exit entry point again, the record should still say "stopped at the exit entry point," rather than infer that someone has become the long-term maintainer for that object.

## Names Still Missing

The `Long-term maintainer` cell remains blank. The old version left it blank because no name was available at the time; it is now left blank to avoid collapsing lab duty, temporary takeover, and interface compatibility checks into a single person's role. The page title can still mislead readers into treating it as the current roster. The page was not renamed or moved in this round to address that issue.

Related cases can be found in QRCA-002, QRCA-005, QRCA-008, and QRCA-011. The entry file is still `docs/adj-qrcoder/ownership/qrcoder-performance-lab-current-maintainer-map.md`.

# Performance Lab Record Divergence Postmortem

This issue started with a mismatch between the compatibility train's record and an old record kept in the performance lab. At first it looked like ordinary result drift: opening the same entry point showed that the capacity table's description had changed, while the quiet zone description still fit with the original procedure. Further comparison revealed that records from two revisions, each labeled "current revision," had been placed at the same entry point, leaving readers unable to tell which one they were seeing.

Those affected were people using that entry point to check the capacity baseline and resource curves. The entry point returned no errors, and no pages were missing; the problem was that it presented two assessments from different times side by side as though they were the same current record. Some people used the old table to explain the changes, while others reviewed them against the new table, so the discussion stalled at "the records are different" rather than the first point of divergence.

| Stage | What we saw at the time | Action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Initial comparison | compatibility train differed from the old record | Initially logged it as a capacity-table change; did not classify it as a generation issue |
| Entry-point review | The current versions of two revisions shared one location | Stopped retrying and preserved the versions as found |
| Follow-up check | quiet zone could be restored | Did not infer that the capacity table had also been restored |

The copy preserved at the time is at `docs/adj-qrcoder/incidents/QRCoder-performance-lab-two-record-versions-not-merged.md`. This was only to let later comparisons return to the text as it stood when the divergence was discovered; it does not mean the two records had been merged. The old assessment next to the entry point was not deleted either: it had treated the capacity-table change as a localized regression, but the shared-entry-point issue discovered later showed that this assessment could not explain the full discrepancy.

Recovery covered only quiet zone. Once it was restored, checks that had depended on that field could resume; why the capacity table had changed, and which consumers had used each revision, went unanswered at the time. This account does not present speculation from adjacent projects as the cause. To investigate again, read the two records separately from the preserved copy, then stop at the first point where the text or generation time differs, rather than attributing all subsequent table differences to a single capacity regression.

This postmortem is still cited because it preserves the state of the entry point when the divergence appeared. It should not be treated as the performance lab's current documentation: "current" here was the label on the entry point at the time, not the version selected after later consolidation.

# Performance Lab Failed Run On-Call Page

This page covers the on-call actions for qrcoder-performance-lab, a failed run. First preserve the incident state, then determine which visible object the failure is associated with; do not use a cleaned-up green result to overwrite the first output. Here, "failed run" refers to the portion of the incident in which one visible result already exists, but it is still not possible to confirm whether a second read, recovery, or collection occurred.

## On Receiving a Run Result

After receiving the message, first save the original input, the version used by the run, the first visible output, and any existing run id (if the incident provides a run id). The record can be placed next to the original result, but do not first refresh permissions, restart execution, or recreate a data set. Those actions will change the location of the first failure and turn a missing item that should have been preserved into new output.

The entry remains `docs/adj-qrcoder/runbooks/QRCoder-performance-lab-failed-run-on-call-page.md`. After opening it, first look for `release evidence`, then check whether this run has a second result. If there is only a final state and no `current revision` from a second run or read, leave that field blank; do not infer from the final state that the second action occurred. QRCA-004 preserve exactly this gap: when the second run or read cannot be recovered, the final state cannot substitute for it.

When the version in the entry file differs from the version shown in the incident, stop at the entry and do not continue with further interpretation. During handoff, include the object name and version seen in the file, as well as the first exception. `DOC-27` is an adjacent migration index; use it only to find the entry relationship, not to substitute for this run's original result. Even if the old entry in the index can still be opened, that does not prove this run started there.

## Find the First Difference First

First select the most recent normal sample. The sample must show the input and version; a record containing only a final state and no raw fragment cannot serve as a normal sample. During comparison, change only one condition: if the input has already been changed, do not also switch the version, redo collection, or switch the output format. If the incident cannot explain what was changed in this run and in the sample respectively, stop at sample selection and leave only the visible versions from both sides.

The goal of the comparison is not to give a cause immediately, but to determine which item differs first. If the inputs are the same but the fragment positions differ, retain both originals; if the inputs and versions both differ, do not compare fragment positions. Later green results on the page, reread results, or internal results must not be written back before the first failure.

### No release evidence

When `release evidence` cannot be found, stop execution; do not first generate missing artifacts or treat a similar file in the directory as evidence for this run. Record the actual path opened, the last version visible, and the output before stopping. If only the final state is visible, return to the "second result" item and keep `current revision` unknown.

If the entry contains that name but this output has no corresponding fragment, treat it as missing as well. Do not assume that this run also generated it just because the entry file contains an old result. This branch only means that on-call cannot continue the assessment using the current material; it does not indicate that the run succeeded, nor does it automatically require a rerun.

### Finder pattern appears

After seeing `finder pattern`, do not clear the incident state. First save the raw fragment containing it, then compare it with the most recent normal sample. At this point, determine only the first difference; do not declare recovery based on it. If the normal sample also lacks the same fragment, stop at sample selection and note the version of each input in the handoff.

If the two inputs are the same but the fragment positions differ, retain both originals and then check the next item; without new raw output, do not use the page color to conclude that the position has recovered. If the fragment disappears after re-execution, still retain the result in which it first appeared. The result from a rerun belongs to a subsequent action and cannot overwrite the original failed fragment.

### Quiet zone, module matrix, and payload

Save the current version of `quiet zone` together with the run input. When it changes, first recheck only this condition; do not also replace `module matrix`, the version, or the output format. If the first difference is in `module matrix`, record the visible objects before and after the difference; do not state insufficient capacity as a conclusion unless the incident itself already provides capacity evidence.

When reviewing the payload, preserve escapes and delimiters; do not manually clean up URL. The confirmed sample is written verbatim as: `MEBKM:TITLE:Example;URL:https\://example.test;;`. This sample is only for checking whether the payload was rewritten and cannot substitute for the failed run's own input; even if the sample passes, it cannot eliminate the difference in `quiet zone` or `module matrix` for this run.

If the input, payload, and version were all changed at the same time, return to the first output and list the one item that could still be confirmed at that time. Do not split multiple changes into post hoc assumed single-variable experiments. A later drill may change only one condition, but its result must be recorded separately under the corresponding step.

### ECI precedence, format interop, and public entry point

If the output does not contain `ECI precedence`, stop there and record "not present" as the incident result. Do not use a successful output in another format to fill in this item. If the issue lies in `format interop`, record the input format, output format, and text of the first failure separately; change only one format condition, and if the result remains unclear, do not continue to the recovery action.

Use `public API` only as a locator term. When you see it, first confirm which public entry segment the current run actually calls; do not treat the internal result as the acceptance result for the ordinary entry just because the entry names are the same. Historical records once showed a case where the internal result had "current result" while the corresponding ordinary entry did not; the fact that the ordinary entry lacked "current result" was later written back, and parallel acceptance of the internal result and ordinary entry was stopped.

During on-call, handle this boundary as follows: if the ordinary entry lacks a result, stop at the ordinary entry and do not cover it with the internal result. If the ordinary entry already has a result but the internal result is missing, do not instead move the ordinary entry's result to the internal result. Keep the two objects beside their respective first outputs until the read or collection for this run can be confirmed.

### first-chance exception, xref offset, and capacity information

When encountering `first-chance exception`, first save the raw exception and the step where it appeared. If there is no stack trace or version, stop at the exception; do not rewrite it as the sole reason the run has failed. If `xref offset` also appears, paste the two fragments into the record in their original order and do not adjust the offset first. If the exception appears first and the offset appears afterward, do not swap their order to make the record look neater.

Enter `capacity table` and `row stride` into the assessment only when the output actually contains these objects. First record which table, row, or stride segment was seen, then compare it with the normal sample for the same input. If there is no corresponding normal sample, stop at the missing sample; do not use default capacity or an empirical value in its place.

Capacity-related objects can appear at the same time as payload and format objects, but do not therefore combine them into one cause. First preserve their positions in the output. If this run does not contain `capacity table` or `row stride`, do not fill in "normal" just to complete the record; this page records only the objects that actually appeared in the incident.

## Stop, Roll Back, and Hand Off

Stop at the current step in all of the following situations: the entry version does not match; there is only a final state and no second action; `release evidence` is missing; the exception has no raw text; two conditions changed in the same drill; or the ordinary entry's result can only be filled in from the internal result. Stopping is not clearing the incident state. Retain the original input, version, first output, and hypotheses that have already been ruled out.

Rollback only undoes actions actually taken during this on-call shift. If the shift did not change data, permissions, or the version, do not perform a "recovery" operation to create a new result; state in the record that shared-environment recovery has not yet been performed. If a reversible action was taken, first return to the entry from before the action, then save the first output after rollback. A successful rollback only means that the incident state returned to its previous state; it does not mean the causes of `finder pattern`, `ECI precedence`, or `format interop` have been confirmed.

The early draft only required finding `release evidence`, not clearing the incident state after seeing `finder pattern`, and stopping when `ECI precedence` was missing; at that time, the recovery action had not yet been tried in the shared environment. Objects not mentioned in the old draft must not be treated as content confirmed by the early run.
