# Temporary Handoff Boundaries for Release Automation

During the handoff, the easiest thing to lose track of isn't the entry point, but who keeps answering once a question reaches the second layer. The release automation on-call entry point can take in an action that has reached its deadline and route the question to the right place; receiving the message first does not make it the long-term owner for API, serialization, or caller behavior.

Record them separately by where the question lands. Here, "original owner" means the person originally responsible for explaining the behavior, not a temporary point of contact or the person coordinating scheduling.

| Incoming issue | First contact | What they can do | Stop here and hand off |
|---|---|---|---|
| An exit action has expired | Temporary maintainer | Confirm whether the action is still within the temporary handoff scope and handle the expired portion. | When an explanation is needed for why release automation produced a particular behavior. |
| The behavior, artifact version, or rollback window of `qrcodertests-release-automation` | Original owner | Explain the existing behavior and determine whether further handling is needed. | When the caller needs to provide the actual usage scenario. |
| The caller sees a different current revision | Release automation on-call entry point | Capture the minimum observed symptoms from both sides and route it for interface-compatibility confirmation. | When someone asks for a cause based only on one side's result. |
| A maintainer entry is missing | The original owner of the relevant object; leave blank if unconfirmed | Fill in only the row for an object that has actually been confirmed. | When the temporary responder would be recorded directly as the long-term owner. |
| Scheduling, time windows, or coordination among multiple people | Coordination contact | Coordinate who looks first and when it is handed back. | When issuing a unified conclusion on technical behavior. |

When the on-call entry point receives a report such as "the current results differ between two environments," first preserve the fact that the two sides really are different. Earlier investigation found no usable command, and later work only added a lead for a command, so the environment difference cannot be recorded as a confirmed release automation cause. When the existing samples cannot distinguish between the two cases, that investigation is over; if the same type of issue comes up again, bring it in through the original entry point rather than continuing to route it based on the old speculation.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Release automation issue received] --> B{Is the exit action expired?}
    B -- Yes --> C[Temporary maintainer handles the expired portion]
    B -- No --> D{Is it asking about the behavior's meaning?}
    D -- Yes --> E[Hand back to the original owner]
    D -- No --> F{Has the maintainer been confirmed?}
    F -- Yes --> G[Contact the maintainer by object]
    F -- No --> H[Keep the slot open and hand off through the on-call entry point]
```

This diagram does not depict "handoff" as a resolution action. It only shows the message's next stop: after the temporary maintainer handles the exit action, they do not automatically take over explaining `qrcodertests-release-automation`; after the original owner receives the behavior question, they likewise do not fill in environment information the caller did not provide. When an issue crosses these boundaries, have the questioner retain the minimum observed symptom, current revision, and observed difference, then let the entry point route it to the next person.

Some issues look like release automation but are actually asking about the meaning of the payload itself. For example, someone may paste `MEBKM:TITLE:Example;URL:https\://example.test;;` and ask whether it is a Bookmark payload; the temporary maintainer is only responsible for confirming that it is not an exit action. The original owner still handles `PayloadGenerator.Bookmark`'s serialization explanation for Example and `https://example.test`. Do not fold serialization semantics into the temporary handoff scope merely because the string appears near the release path.

The blank slot marked `payload serializer` in the old table therefore remains, but its meaning needs to be made explicit: the blank slot is not a prompt for the on-call person to explain the payload themselves; it signals a handback to the behavior owner. `rectangle run` still requires the caller to provide a name; without the caller's identity, the issue cannot be assigned to a particular maintainer. The long-term handoff owner for `module matrix` is also still unconfirmed. The coordination contact can drive the confirmation but does not occupy this slot.

Several cards serve only as indexes into this page; they do not each establish a separate responsibility table:

- QRCB-003 previously recorded the handling direction "route the caller's issue to the person responsible for interface compatibility for confirmation," along with the record that results differed between two environments and the command had not yet been found. It is suitable for bringing the issue, with its minimum observed symptom, into the on-call entry point.
- The scope of QRCB-005 is limited to replacing only one adjacent `qrcodertests-release-automation`; all other entry points remain unchanged. It cannot, on that basis, designate a long-term maintainer.
- QRCB-012 requires leaving the current revision unknown until it is confirmed that collection or execution actually occurred. When an incoming issue contains only a version guess, do not claim ownership first just to fill in the table.
- QRCB-014 requires timestamping the old assessment and then appending the new release automation result alongside it. Record responsibility changes the same way: do not erase the old row; add a new row with the object and handoff scope.

The minimum handoff information for a temporary handoff is the object name, current revision, first visible difference, and whether the issue has been clearly identified as an exit action. If this information is enough to determine that the action has expired, the temporary maintainer can complete this part of the work; if it is not enough to explain the behavior, do not write "continue investigating" as the temporary owner's long-term responsibility. After the original owner answers the behavior question, whether the blank slot needs to be updated is a separate matter; change the table only once the handoff relationship has been confirmed.

The entry point is still `docs/adj-qrcodertests/ownership/adj-qrcodertests-interim-ownership-boundaries.md`. This records the boundaries during the temporary release automation handoff; it does not replace the project's own main text, attachments, or rollback-window records.

The comparison in QRCC-009 requires qrcoderdemouwp-client-integration, the current entry point, and the command to remain fixed, with only the current revision replaced. The point is to narrow the change to the revision; if the entry point or input changes, or a different extension path is used, the resulting difference no longer counts as this round's comparison. The page should record the respective revisions before and after replacement and the first difference, rather than write "looks normal" as the result.

QRCC-019 was later marked complete, but this page did not retain the actual user's name or the details of the repeat check. Therefore, only the verification method remains here: have an actual user follow the original entry point to the current revision and stop at the first difference. A completion status can only indicate that this work record has ended; it cannot fill in the missing repeat-check details on the page.

Break it down first. Follow-up notes should go on the original page and state whether they concern the entry point, the revision comparison, or the rollback and exit action; do not combine the three kinds of records into a single pass or a single failure. # Public Entry Point Maintenance Decision

When this page was first created, the dispute sounded like a very small entry-point adjustment: should the current `raster-text-renderers` entry point remain on the path shared by the team, or should it be changed during this window? In hindsight, the entry-point name, file location, and format behavior were described at the time as one thing, but were actually three different things. They happened to appear in the same round of discussion, but cannot substitute for one another.

The clues that could be checked at the time were `QRCoder/QRCodeGenerator.cs` and several call names. The record included the terms text, bytes, matrix, public, format, require, small, payload, result. These terms show that someone examined local relationships along that path, but do not show that the file location is a permanent home, nor that an entry-point name has already constituted a format commitment. The earliest draft did not make this distinction clear; it only said "leave it unchanged for now," which is easy to read as treating retention of the entry point as joint confirmation of the implementation and compatibility.

This addendum does not turn the old conclusion into a new interface specification. It preserves the original decision while spelling out separately the two approaches actually compared at the time: on one side, keeping the current entry point; on the other, adjusting the entry point within the window. Each side had its reasons, as well as gaps that had not been filled at the time.

## Two Approaches Considered in Review

The direct benefit of keeping the current entry point is that the team's existing lookup point does not suddenly stop working after this round of review. When someone is locating a problem through the entry point and call names, the entry point remains where it was, making it easier to continue collaborating than with a temporary rename or move. This benefit concerns only the shared entry point for this round; it does not mean that every type of output under the entry point has been confirmed.

Keeping it also has clear costs. The old name will continue to be used, and a name is easily read as a commitment broader than the actual evidence supports. Especially in format discussions, if someone treats a successful return, the existence of an object, or a screenshot as a basis for compatibility, retaining the entry point makes this misreading harder to detect. The review did not expand any format judgment on the grounds that "the entry point is still there."

The benefit of an adjustment window is that the entry-point boundaries can be rearranged, making it clearer when the old entry point remains usable and when it can be withdrawn. But at the time this option had only a direction, not enough executable detail: there was no defined window, no recorded withdrawal point, and no material that could show the affected scope. The meeting's requirement to retain "a withdrawable old entry point" did not mean that these conditions already existed.

Therefore, the adjustment window was not approved as part of this round's decision. This conclusion does not mean that an adjustment would necessarily cause problems; it means that there was not enough basis at the time to write "may be adjusted later" as "has now been adjusted." The objections were kept in the decision rather than deleted just to close things out.

## How Far Approval Went at the Time

The decision criterion in the meeting materials was:

> The team treats emitted bytes and matrix geometry as public behavior, so format claims require a small reproducible payload and an independently parsed result.

This statement limited the scope that could be approved at the time. Emitted bytes and matrix geometry were treated as part of public behavior; therefore, claims about format required a small, reproducible payload and an independently parsed result. It did not require rechecking all formats at once, nor did it turn any particular call name into proof of compatibility.

In early discussions, there was a more expedient formulation: as long as the entry point could still return result, let the format judgment pass for now. The review did not adopt this formulation. result is one of the objects that needs to be examined, but its existence alone is insufficient to show that the contents of emitted bytes or the matrix geometry match external format expectations. Conversely, seeing a matrix object cannot replace independent parsing. The several objects must correspond to one another on the same small sample before they are sufficient to support a specific format judgment.

This also explains why the review did not write "retain the entry point" as "maintain full compatibility." The former addresses where the team enters and continues looking in this round; the latter concerns whether specific outputs can be independently identified based on external results. The two are related, but they are not the same decision. Compressing them into the sentence "there is no problem with the current entry point" would lose the actual limitation on the scope approved in this round.

## Decision Made

The decision itself was narrow: retain the current `raster-text-renderers` entry point and do not adjust it during this round's window. The condition for retaining it was that the old entry point should remain replaceable by a later switch, rather than being written up as an untouchable fixed location. The meeting required the actual impact, a coordinator, and a withdrawable old entry point to be recorded precisely because the entry-point choice would affect subsequent collaboration, but there still was not enough to declare a migration complete at the time.

The coordination arrangement served only this local decision. The integration side brought the discussion and review together at the same entry point; the build side additionally checked the code paths and output materials; the platform side additionally checked results that could be confirmed at runtime. This arrangement is not an ownership map for the entry point, nor does it mean that the three parties jointly guaranteed the unconfirmed portions. When the objects seen by different people do not match, the record should preserve the discrepancy rather than cover it up with a new name.

At the time, the actual impact could only be stated this far: discussions that depend on the current lookup path could continue using the old entry point; anyone wanting to make a format judgment needed to bring a small payload and an independently parsed result; anyone advocating an adjustment to the entry point needed to provide the window and the boundary for withdrawing the old entry point. No material showed that any category of caller had completed migration, and no material showed that a new entry-point name had been determined.

## Objections Left on Record

The side opposed to immediate adjustment worried that the dispute at the entry-point level had not yet been disentangled; changing the window first would make existing callers lose their familiar lookup point without simultaneously adding material that could be checked. This concern supported "keep it for now," but cannot prove that the retention approach would remain appropriate later.

The side opposed to continued retention worried that the longer the old entry point remained, the easier it would be to conflate its name with its actual behavior. This concern was not overturned by this round's decision either. In particular, if someone reduced format compatibility to "the call succeeds" or "there is a result," the old entry point would be mistaken for a commitment broader than what it actually carries.

The two opinions point to different risks. The former is concerned with whether the switch itself would interrupt the shared entry point; the latter with whether retaining it would create an overly broad statement about behavior. The review did not try to eliminate both concerns with a single conclusion, so the earlier objections remain on file. They are not substitutes for action items, nor are they an evaluation of any particular implementation location.

## Review Addendum

The follow-up review first corrected the judgments that had been conflated earlier. The file location remains a clue checked at the time; the team entry point remains retained under this round's decision; whether the format behavior holds still has to be assessed against payload, emitted bytes, matrix geometry, and an independently parsed result. The review did not recombine these three items into a more emphatic conclusion.

The review also retained a stopping point: when there are only call names, screenshots, or a single returned result, the scope of approval cannot be expanded just because the entry point was not adjusted. What is needed is not a longer explanation, but material that lets the same payload be independently parsed. If new samples are obtained later, they should state which judgment they changed, rather than retroactively writing this round's retention decision as already covering all outputs.

The original draft's "keep it for now, then revisit whether to adjust once the window is clear" remains here. It was the working position at the time and should not be taken out on its own as proof of the current implementation or all format relationships. The limitations added after it here explain that this sentence addresses only whether the entry point changes immediately; it does not address all behavior, nor does it provide an already-implemented switching step.

As of this review, the record still contains no concrete arrangement for the adjustment window, no new entry-point name, and no migration batch. A withdrawable old entry point is a condition the review required to be retained, not a handoff that has already been completed. Explicitly leaving the gap is closer to the decision at the time than filling it in as a conclusion using the coordination arrangement.

The DOC-44 item is a separate copy of the local materials for the entry-point switch handoff; it can help continue handling the handoff, but does not replace the two options, reasons for deferral, and objections left here.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Current entry point] --> B[Retained this round]
    B --> C[Small payload]
    C --> D[emitted bytes and matrix geometry]
    D --> E[Independently parsed result]
    A -.Adjustment window not approved.-> F[Fill in the adjustment window and withdrawal boundary]
```

The order in the diagram expresses only the relationship recorded in this round: the entry point is retained first, and a specific format judgment still needs to return to a small sample and independent parsing. It does not indicate that a new release, migration, or entry-point adjustment has been completed.

# Public Entry Point Maintenance Cutover Handoff

Added here after review: Keep the old entry point in place. The cutover starts with an inventory of the known consumers of shared-library-support. Don't roll out the candidate path broadly; first choose one consumer that can roll back on its own to try it. This lets that consumer return to the old entry point if the trial fails, without also moving over integrations that haven't been confirmed.

```text
Old entry point ──Known consumers──> Candidate path
   ^                                    |
   └──── Roll back if the trial fails ──┘
```

This review confirmed that the handoff package must contain at least three things: the exact public entry point, one boundary example, and a consumer or parser that can independently confirm that entry point. Providing only the candidate path does not count as completion; if a consumer has already switched paths but the consumer or parser still can't confirm it, keep the status as migration in progress as well.

Steps, in order:
- List the known consumers still using the old entry point;
- Choose one of them that can roll back on its own to try the candidate path;
- Include the public entry point and boundary example in the handoff to the recipient, and have the consumer or parser confirm independently;
- If confirmation fails, roll back that consumer and keep the old entry point available.

The file-tracing notes for the entry point are recorded separately in DOC-45. The inventory results haven't been added here yet; without the inventory and rollback action, don't mark the cutover complete.

encoding-engine

  -> The first real consumer in the team public entry point maintenance window

If you need to determine whether an actual run went through this path, then check the entry point, run id, trace, or version against the original execution records. Execution records can show what that run went through; they cannot, on their own, substitute for call relationships between files.

# encoding-engine Entry-Point Tracing Notes

`QRCoder/QRCodeGenerator/EncodingMode.cs` is the first file this trace can be anchored to. The early notes started from the public entry-point name `encoding-engine` and stopped here after finding the filename and a match for `encoding`. What they left was not a module overview, but a narrow path for the next person to follow. This starting point is still retained because it connects the search terms to an actual object in the repository; it does not explain the entire encoding workflow.

## What to look for in the file first

Start by reading the encoding modes declared by `EncodingMode.cs` itself and the adjacent references. Don't start by opening up every file under `QRCodeGenerator` directory by directory, or treat files as callers just because their names are similar. Look for the direct relationships needed for the next hop: which entry point reads the mode here, where locally that read occurs, and whether the call name still lines up in the public entry points further along.

Confirm the direct caller from a use site, rather than inferring it from a filename. Once you've found the use site, look back at the values the caller passes in, retains, or transforms. If a caller merely contains the same encoding term without reading this mode, it is still only a search signpost. The available material does not give this caller a stable name that can be used long-term, so recording the relationship is safer than forcing in an object name.

The early draft was terse, saying only, "Continue from the file by following the call name." This sentence was unpacked during the later review because "following the call name" could lead to mistaking search results for call edges. The actual code-reading order was changed to:

```text
encoding-engine
      |
      v
QRCoder/QRCodeGenerator/EncodingMode.cs
      |
      | Follow only one direct call
      v
Direct caller
      |
      | See which public entry point it carries the encoding mode to
      v
First actual consumer in the maintenance window for the team's shared entry point
```

The direct caller in the diagram is not a fixed object you can infer from a filename. First find it at a use site of `EncodingMode.cs`, then look back at the values the caller passes in, retains, or transforms. Only after confirming this step should you continue along the public entry point to examine the first actual consumer. Files with the same name but no call edge are not part of this path; at most, they help you locate the file again.

## How to carry out a trace

After starting from the entry point, you only need to retain three pieces of local information. First, the name of the encoding mode actually read in `EncodingMode.cs`; second, the direct caller's call site and which of the team's shared entry points it passes this choice to; third, the entry-point name of the first actual consumer. These three items represent different levels; one search result cannot stand in for the other two.

If you need to determine whether a run actually passed through this chain, cross-check the corresponding run id, trace, or version against the raw execution records. Check the entry-point name and version in the records first, then return to the code to confirm the file relationships. An entry point appearing in the records can only help locate an actual run; it cannot prove a direct call between two files just because they look adjacent in the sequence. Conversely, a use site in the code does not mean every run passes through it.

When you encounter files with the same name, return to the second piece of information first. Continue only with those that can be matched through code adjacency or raw execution records; files that only turn up in search results and have no call edge remain signposts. Don't add unseen intermediate layers just to make the path look complete. If the direct caller already shows the public entry point, but the first actual consumer still requires clarification from those maintaining the team's shared entry point, stop the record at the consumer boundary and retain the entry-point name.

Here, "first actual consumer" means the object already receiving the handoff from that public entry point, whose maintenance relationship still needs to be explained. It is not the first file you see, nor an owner you can infer from the directory hierarchy. If only the entry-point name can be confirmed, put only that name in the body. If the next hop depends on an explanation from another owner, don't fill the gap with a similar module name. The path left behind may be short, but the next person will know which object to ask about next.

## Early assessment and later changes

The early version all but equated "finding the file" with "finding the entry point," so it did not distinguish the file location, direct calls, and actual consumption. That assessment has not been removed: it explains why old links or search results lead people to `EncodingMode.cs`, and why a path diagram was added during the later review. It can now only be treated as the early interpretation of the code, not as grounds for assigning permanent maintenance ownership based on file location.

The reviewed path confirms only the segment "file—one direct caller—the first actual consumer in the maintenance window for the team's shared entry point." It does not connect all encoding modes, all possible callers, or public entry points across the entire workspace. Broadening the search adds candidates, not automatically more confirmed relationships; this page therefore still retains only one direct call.

The review of `EncodingMode.cs` also changed the recording order: first confirm the local use site, then examine how the caller passes the mode to the public entry point, and only then use raw execution records to check the execution trail. This keeps "adjacency present in the code" separate from "an entry point actually traversed by a particular run." When both kinds of material are available, use each for the questions it can answer; they do not substitute for each other.

For deviation records from the maintenance window for the team's shared entry point, see [DOC-46](DOC-46). That page retains anomalous timing changes within the window; this page retains only the trace path from `encoding-engine` to the first actual consumer. You can navigate between the two pages, but don't retroactively apply conclusions from the anomaly records to this code relationship.

After reaching the first actual consumer, the trace ends here if the next step needs an explanation from another owner.

# Public Entry Maintenance Deviation Postmortem

This deviation occurred during the Team Public Entry Maintenance window. The result observed on site did not match the original plan, and the handoff personnel were temporarily unable to tell whether to continue using the original entry point or treat the difference as meaning the switchover was complete. The record did not classify it at the time as a failure in any particular stage; it was initially handled as an anomaly requiring a pause.

## Incident timeline

- After maintenance began, the first finding was that the entry point as presented did not match the original plan. The visible result was already enough to affect confirmation during the shift, but there was no evidence indicating whether the deviation came from the maintenance action, the entry-point configuration, or a later stage.
- During the discussion, continuing to use the new result was considered first. This judgment was based on the page seen on site, not on a status record that had been verified; it was later discovered that different handoff participants had not received exactly the same entry point, so the switch scope was not expanded further.
- The old entry point was retained during temporary recovery. It could still be withdrawn at the time and allowed the handoff to continue, so it was used first to restore a usable state. This action only addressed the blocker for that shift; it did not explain why the on-site result deviated from the original plan.
- After recovery, the raw execution record was preserved, and the follow-up note recorded the actual impact, the coordinator, and the conditions for withdrawing the old entry point. Here, "recovery" means that handoffs could continue via the entry point; it does not mean the root cause had been determined.

## Impact

Those affected were the people who relied on the public entry point to confirm status during the maintenance window. When the original plan, the on-site result, and the temporary entry point were all present at once, handoff personnel could reach opposite conclusions depending on which entry point they used. The confirmed impact was that the verification path became inconsistent; there is no material showing that the implementation itself changed more broadly as a result, nor was the deviation generalized into a claim that all entry points were unavailable.

One early working judgment at the time was that retaining the old entry point was equivalent to completing recovery. That statement later proved too broad. The old entry point provided only a temporary fallback that could be withdrawn; it could not replace verification of the new result. Because, when this postmortem was prepared, the maintenance action, entry-point configuration, and later stages still had not been correlated one by one, the cause remains unconfirmed.

## Tracing lead

During the shift, the source of the entry point was searched for using the call name for `QRCoderDemo/Properties/Resources.Designer.cs`. That was a tracing lead at the time, not a confirmed permanent ownership assignment; this record therefore retains the file location and the judgment made then, rather than presenting the source-code location as the final explanation for this public-entry deviation.

# Troubleshooting Inconsistent Public Entry Results

The ticket says Team Public Entry Maintenance is complete, but the results for the same input still cannot be verified. First check the call entry point and version for matrix-serialization; don't prematurely treat the two results as one conclusion.

```text
Inconsistent results
├─ Entry point and version known?
│  ├─ No: fill in these two items; stop
│  └─ Yes: retrieve the raw execution record for the same input
└─ Records comparable?
   ├─ Yes: record the actual impact, then check whether the old entry point can be withdrawn
   └─ No: coordinator supplements the record; stop
```

First record the actual impact, the coordinator, and whether the old entry point can be withdrawn. The available material is insufficient to show which side is correct; do not use repeated runs as a vote.

# Troubleshooting Inconsistent Results from the Shared Entry Point

The ticket says "Team shared-entry-point maintenance is complete," but the result for the same input still cannot be verified. Don't treat it as complete yet; first confirm the call entry point and version of matrix-serialization. If the entry point is unclear, fill in only these two items; don't investigate based on other guesses.

This time, the raw execution records for the same input were reviewed side by side. Records cannot substitute for entry-point information: if the version is unknown, the difference has no basis for comparison; if the entry point is known but the records are missing, repeated execution still cannot determine which side is trustworthy.

```text
Inconsistent results
├─ Are the call entry point and version known?
│  ├─ No: fill in the entry point and version; stop
│  └─ Yes: retrieve the raw execution records for the same input
└─ Are the two records comparable?
   ├─ Yes: record the actual impact; confirm whether the old entry point can be rolled back
   └─ No: log the missing records; the coordinator takes ownership; stop
```

This round did not establish a new cause. First check whether the two records correspond to the same input; if they do not, log only the gap; do not infer the entry point from the result contents. If the entry point is known but the versions differ, record only the difference; this does not determine which result is correct. Compare only after the records are complete; if the comparison requires a new owner, stop there too.

At this point, record the actual impact, the coordinator, and the old entry point that can be rolled back. For the actual impact, first write down who received different results; don't add guesses. If the old entry point cannot be rolled back, keep it on the branch; don't overwrite it with the new result. When new evidence or a new owner is needed, the tree ends here; do not use repeated reruns as a vote.
